title: Varicose veins: from valve failure to the right treatment
subject: surgery
summary: Find out why varicose veins form, how to examine and image them, and which treatment the exam and current practice each expect.

objectives.text: Name the commonest vein, reflux site and type of varicose veins, and apply the CEAP 3 mm definition
Predict flow direction through perforators and what the calf pump does to leg venous pressure in reflux
Place the great and short saphenous veins and the named perforators (Cockett, Boyd, Dodd, Hunter) correctly
Pick the nerve at risk for GSV versus SSV surgery and the lower limit of GSV stripping
Place a venous ulcer by site and tell skin changes and CEAP classes apart
Tell the Brodie-Trendelenburg test from the Perthes test and read each result
Decide whether superficial vein surgery can go ahead by checking deep vein patency first
Choose the investigation of choice and the role of Doppler and venography
Pick the first-line treatment of truncal reflux, the next step if unsuitable, and who gets stockings
Choose foam versus liquid sclerotherapy and the sclerosant (STS or polidocanol)
Pick the step before compression for a venous ulcer, its mainstay treatment and the malignancy to biopsy for
Tell a saphena varix from a femoral hernia at the bedside

traps.trap: Trendelenburg operation with stripping is the first-line treatment for SFJ incompetence
A bedside Doppler, clinical test or venography is the investigation of choice for varicose veins (merged TR3: venography stretched to superficial reflux)
The Perthes test detects SFJ incompetence and the Brodie-Trendelenburg test detects deep vein patency
On the Brodie-Trendelenburg test, filling with the tourniquet still on means SFJ incompetence
The Trendelenburg test, operation, position and sign are one thing
The great and short saphenous veins run and terminate the same way
The saphenous nerve is at risk in short saphenous surgery; the sural nerve in GSV stripping
The GSV is stripped all the way to the ankle
Named perforators are interchangeable or placed at the wrong level
Perforator valves let blood flow from deep to superficial veins
Walking raises venous pressure in the leg; the calf pump produces ambulatory venous hypertension
CEAP diameter bands and ulcer-class numbers are interchangeable (merged TR15: C4, C5, C6 order)
Compression is started for a venous ulcer without measuring ABPI first
Compression stockings are the treatment for symptomatic varicose veins
Superficial vein stripping or ligation can be done without checking the deep veins
The most common finding is the only one (SFJ is the only site of reflux; primary is the only type)
Foam sclerotherapy suits telangiectasias; liquid sclerotherapy suits large truncal veins
Polidocanol is wrong as the sclerosant because the classic answer is STS
A saphena varix and a femoral hernia share a fluid thrill and both disappear on lying down
A venous ulcer sits on the toes, heel or lateral malleolus (the arterial sites)

say.text: A 52-year-old teacher has bulging veins running from the groin down the inner thigh to the ankle.
Before we teach anything: where would you expect the reflux to start?

choices.label: At the saphenopopliteal junction, where the great saphenous ends
At the saphenofemoral junction, the most frequent site
At the saphenofemoral junction, the only site
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about where the great saphenous vein ends, and which vein it drains into.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because 'most frequent' sounds like 'the only', but a superlative ranks sites; it does not exclude the others.
Read the question again as asking for the commonest site, not the sole one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the superlative is the word to re-read. Ranking and exclusion are different claims.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the two saphenous veins are easy to blur into one template.
They share a name and a starting area at the dorsal venous arch, but not a course or an end.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin down which side each vein runs on before you trust its termination.

say.text: Yes. The saphenofemoral junction is the most common site of reflux, where the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein.
Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins, 3 mm or more across when standing. The great saphenous system is the most commonly affected.
The most common site of reflux is the saphenofemoral junction, and primary veins are the most common type. Secondary veins follow deep vein thrombosis, pelvic masses or an AV fistula.
The great saphenous runs in front of the medial malleolus and joins the femoral vein. The short saphenous runs behind the lateral malleolus and usually joins the popliteal vein.
A registrar says: 'Most varicose veins are primary, so primary is the only kind we see.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Primary veins are the only kind that occurs
Primary veins are commonest, but secondary veins also occur
Secondary veins are less common, so they do not occur
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what 'most common' ranks, and whether a lower rank can still mean that something happens.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because 'most common' reads as 'the only', so every other type drops out of the picture.
Other types still occur, with causes such as deep vein thrombosis or an AV fistula.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read 'most common': it ranks the types, it does not list the only one.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a lower rank can feel like an absence, so 'less common' slides into 'does not occur'.
Secondary varicose veins are a real type with identifiable causes, so the ranking does not remove them.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read 'less common': it ranks the types, it does not deny them.

say.text: Yes. Primary veins are the most common type, and secondary veins follow deep vein thrombosis, pelvic masses or an AV fistula.
Which description fits the short saphenous vein?

choices.label: In front of the medial malleolus, joining the popliteal vein
Behind the lateral malleolus, joining the popliteal vein
Behind the lateral malleolus, joining the femoral vein
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start from the dorsal venous arch: which end, medial or lateral, does the short saphenous begin from?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the two veins' sides get swapped while the popliteal end is kept.
Side and termination belong to one vein, so check the side first, then the termination.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the side is the anchor: the short saphenous's side is the one that goes with its termination.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because it names the right side, but the femoral end belongs to the great saphenous.
Check which end this vein joins before you trust the side.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the termination is the check: the femoral end is the other vein's.

say.text: The short saphenous begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, runs behind the lateral malleolus and usually joins the popliteal vein.
The great saphenous begins at the medial end, runs in front of the medial malleolus and joins the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction.
Yes. The short saphenous begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, runs behind the lateral malleolus and usually joins the popliteal vein.
A 48-year-old woman has a varicose calf, and duplex shows one perforator that no longer closes properly.
Before I explain, predict. In a normal leg, which way does blood cross a perforator?

choices.label: Deep into superficial, through the one-way valve
Superficial into deep, through the one-way valve
Deep into superficial, pushed by the calf squeeze
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because reflux, the disease you are reading about, runs from deep to superficial.
But reflux is the failure of the valve, not its design. Ask what a healthy perforator valve is there to do, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the words: reflux and normal describe opposite states of the same valve.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the calf squeeze really does move blood, so the push feels like the direction.
But the squeeze is only the force. The valve decides the direction, so ask which way that valve lets blood through in a healthy leg, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but the squeeze is the force and the valve is the gate.

say.text: Hint: a perforator links the two systems. In a healthy leg the valve is there to stop blood falling back from one of them. Which one?
Yes. Perforating veins link the superficial and deep systems, and their valves normally let blood pass only from superficial to deep.
Now the calf. You stand, then you walk. In a normal leg, what does the calf muscle pump do to venous pressure in the leg?

choices.label: Pushes it up, each time the calf squeezes
Lowers it, each time the calf squeezes
Raises it, and it stays high while walking
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the squeeze you feel in the calf looks like a push, and the leg feels heavy when you stand.
But one squeeze is a moment. The question is the pressure across the whole walk, and that is what the pump controls. Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the timescale: the pump's job shows up in the pressure across the walk.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the leg feels swollen and tight after standing, so the pressure must be high all the time.
But that describes the symptom, not the pump's action. Ask what the pump does to pressure on each walk in a healthy leg, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, and this mix-up is common: symptoms come on with standing, but the pump is not working backwards.

say.text: Hint: think about the pump's job, not the symptom. The leg's pump is there to clear blood out of the lower leg each time you walk.
Yes. The calf muscle pump lowers venous pressure in the leg each time you walk.

choices.label: Show me what happens when it fails
I know this, skip the explanation

say.text: When reflux or a blocked deep vein stops that fall, the pressure stays high on walking. That is ambulatory venous hypertension.
Sustained high pressure leaks fluid, red cells and fibrinogen into the tissues. That causes the oedema, skin change and ulcers you will meet next.
A 55-year-old with a long-standing varicose leg. Her ankle venous pressure does not fall when she walks.
Which state is this, and why?

choices.label: A normal exercise response, as pressure rises and then settles
Ambulatory venous hypertension, from reflux or deep obstruction
Ambulatory venous hypertension, since the pump pushes pressure up

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the word pump suggests it drives pressure up, and the name sounds like a push.
But a healthy pump does not push pressure up on walking. Here the question is why the pressure stays high, so ask what failed to happen. Choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the cause: the state name fits, but the pump's role in it is reversed.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a brief rise in pressure on exercise is real, so it looks like a normal response.
But this patient's pressure does not fall afterwards, and that failure to fall is the whole finding. Compare the two legs, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at the vignette again: the pressure that never falls is the clue.

say.text: Yes. The pump should lower pressure on walking. With reflux or deep obstruction it cannot, so the pressure stays high: ambulatory venous hypertension.
Last check on the valve itself. Which statement about a perforator valve is true?

choices.label: It closes when blood tries to flow from deep to superficial
It closes when blood tries to flow from superficial to deep

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because you may remember reflux as blood going the wrong way, so the reverse wording feels like the rule.
But reflux is the failure, not the rule. Check which way a healthy valve must shut to stop the reflux you read about, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the direction of closure: reflux is the failure of exactly that closure.

say.text: Yes. A healthy perforator valve opens only from superficial to deep, so it shuts against blood going from deep to superficial. That shutting is what fails in reflux.
Now the named perforators. Which one sits at the medial ankle, linking the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Boyd is on the medial leg, but it sits just below the knee, not at the ankle.
Place each name at its own level on the leg, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the level: the names are not interchangeable on the leg.

say.text: That choice is not right. Hunter sits at mid-thigh, far above the ankle you were asked about.
Check the level of the ankle perforator, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the level: a name at the thigh cannot be the ankle one.

say.text: Hint: start at the ankle and walk up the inner side of the leg, naming each perforator you pass.
Yes. Cockett sits at the medial ankle, connecting the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins.
Now the order. Put the four medial perforators in order, from the ankle up to the mid-thigh.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the four names all sit on the medial leg, so their order feels arbitrary.
But check where Dodd sits against the knee, and where Boyd sits, before you choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so climb the leg again: the order is set by level, not by the names.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because it is the same four names read from the thigh down, which looks like a tidy list.
But the question climbs from the ankle, and this list runs the other way. Start at the ankle and climb one level at a time, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the start point: the climb begins at the ankle, not the thigh.

say.text: Hint: begin with the lowest of the four, on the ankle, and name the next one you reach each time you go up a level.
Yes. Climbing from the ankle: Cockett at the ankle, Boyd just below the knee, Dodd in the lower thigh, and Hunter at mid-thigh.
Take the great saphenous vein (GSV) and the small saphenous vein (SSV). Which pair of courses is correct?

choices.label: Great runs lateral, ends popliteal; small runs medial, ends femoral
Great runs medial, ends femoral; small runs lateral, ends popliteal
Both run medial and end in the femoral vein
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because both veins start at the dorsal venous arch, so they seem to share one course that only swaps at the ends.
But they leave the arch on opposite sides of the ankle and end in different veins. Check which malleolus each one passes, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the side: where a vein starts does not decide where it runs.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the two veins share a start point, so they feel like one vein with one course.
But they run on opposite sides of the leg and end in different veins. Name the malleolus each one passes, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the template: two veins from one arch are not one course.

say.text: Hint: start both veins at the dorsal venous arch, then ask which malleolus each one passes on the way up.
Yes. The great saphenous vein runs in front of the medial malleolus and joins the femoral vein. The small one runs behind the lateral malleolus and usually joins the popliteal vein.
Four medial perforators, from the ankle up. Cockett sits at the medial ankle and lower leg, linking the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins.
Boyd sits just below the knee, Dodd in the lower thigh, and Hunter at mid-thigh.
A 58-year-old woman has a shallow ulcer just above her inner ankle. The skin around it is brown, and her ankle is swollen.
What type of ulcer is this?

choices.label: Arterial ulcer, since the ankle is a pressure point
Neuropathic ulcer, since the ankle bears weight
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the skin around the ulcer, then ask where venous pressure is highest in a standing leg.
Yes. Venous ulcers form in the gaiter area, just above the medial malleolus.
Leaked red cells leave haemosiderin behind, and that is what stains the skin brown.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because many ankle and foot ulcers are filed under arterial disease by default.
Brown skin is haemosiderin from leaked red cells, and ankle swelling is a venous symptom. Read those clues again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the skin and the swelling are the clues to weigh before the site.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a weight-bearing ankle makes pressure-site ulcers come to mind.
Nothing in this case points to pressure. Haemosiderin from leaked red cells is what stains this skin brown.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the skin change before reaching for a pressure cause.

say.text: Three leg ulcers are seen in clinic: one just above the inner ankle, one on the heel and one on the tip of a toe.
Which one is the venous ulcer?

choices.label: The ulcer on the heel, which bears weight
The ulcer on the tip of a toe
The ulcer just above the inner ankle
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where the venous pressure of a standing leg is highest, then which of the three ulcers sits there.
Yes. Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area, just above the medial malleolus. Learn that site as the venous one to recognise first.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because a heel is the spot that takes the most load, so it looks like a pressure ulcer.
The question asks for the venous site, which has its own named position. Read it again and check which site that is.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read what the question asks: the venous site, not the one under most load.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a toe-tip wound is the classic foot ulcer most people picture first.
Venous ulcers are a lower-leg site, not a toe-tip site. Read the question again and pick the one that fits.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the toe is the foot picture talking. Match the venous site to the lower leg.

say.text: A 47-year-old man has a tortuous vein on the calf that he can see standing up.
In CEAP, which diameter measured standing makes a vein varicose, in class C2?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Telangiectasias and reticular veins together make class C1. Which diameter marks the step up to C2?
Yes. Varicose veins are subcutaneous veins 3 mm or more in diameter, measured standing.
Telangiectasias are under 1 mm and reticular veins 1 to 3 mm. Together they form class C1, not C2.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because 1 mm sits on the edge of the reticular band, so the number feels familiar.
Reticular veins are C1, and that band runs from 1 to 3 mm. Varicose veins are a different class, so ask where C2 starts.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the bands apart: each diameter belongs to a class, not to one threshold.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the smallest band is the first one most students memorise.
Telangiectasias are under 1 mm and are class C1. Varicose veins need a larger diameter, so choose the one that gives it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the smallest band from the varicose threshold.

say.text: A 60-year-old man had a venous ulcer that closed last month. Today no ulcer is open on his leg.
Which CEAP class fits him?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether an ulcer is still open today, then find the class that names that state.
Yes. A healed venous ulcer is C5, and an active one is C6.
C4 names the skin changes themselves, so skin signs and ulcer state are separate classes.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because skin changes often sit beside a healed ulcer, so C4 feels like the label.
C4 names the skin signs (C4a, b and c). The question asks about the ulcer's state, so ask which class names that state.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the question is about the ulcer's state, not the skin around it.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because C5 and C6 sit side by side and are easy to swap.
C6 is the active ulcer class. Check whether an ulcer is open today, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the open-or-closed state decides between the two ulcer classes.

say.text: A lower leg is shaped like an inverted champagne bottle, with hard, thick skin and fat above the ankle.
Which CEAP subclass describes this skin?

choices.label: C4c, a fan of ankle veins
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which subclass names induration of the skin and fat of the lower leg, the hard sign rather than colour or small veins?
Yes. Lipodermatosclerosis is induration and fibrosis of the skin and fat of the lower leg, giving the inverted champagne bottle shape.
C4a is pigmentation or eczema, and C4c is corona phlebectatica, a fan of small veins around the ankle.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because pigmentation is the skin sign most people spot first.
Pigmentation and eczema are C4a, but this leg describes hard, thick skin. Which subclass names that?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the word 'hard' is the one to match, not the colour.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the ankle is where corona phlebectatica sits, so the site looks right.
Corona phlebectatica is a fan of small veins, not hard, thick skin. Which subclass names the induration?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the site matches, but the skin change does not. Check the skin first.

say.text: A 66-year-old woman has a groin swelling. It pushes out on coughing and goes down when she lies flat. Tapping it gives a fluid thrill.
What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Femoral hernia through the femoral canal
Saphena varix of the great saphenous vein
Inguinal hernia through the inguinal canal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Both diagnoses share the cough impulse and the change on lying flat. Ask which feature only one of them shows on tapping.
Yes. A saphena varix is a dilated great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction, with a cough impulse and a fluid thrill on tapping.
A cough impulse alone does not separate it from a hernia. The fluid thrill on tapping, and emptying on lying down, do.
That choice is not right. Both a hernia and a saphena varix give a cough impulse and go down on lying flat.
Those shared signs cannot separate them. The fluid thrill on tapping is the feature a hernia does not give.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the thrill: the cough impulse is the feature the two diagnoses share.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because any groin swelling with a cough impulse gets filed as a hernia.
Check the feature this case adds beyond the cough impulse, then choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the case adds more than a cough impulse. Weigh the added feature.

say.text: A femoral hernia is bowel or fat through the femoral canal. It has a cough impulse, but tapping it gives no fluid thrill.
A saphena varix is a dilated great saphenous vein at the junction. It has a cough impulse and a fluid thrill, and it empties on lying down.
A leg with varicose veins. You raise the leg to empty the veins, press firmly over the saphenofemoral junction, and ask the patient to stand.
With the pressure still on, the veins fill again from below. Which structure is letting blood in?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The junction is squeezed, so blood cannot arrive from above. Where else could blood reach the superficial veins?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the junction is the spot you pressed, so it looks like the leak.
But the pressure sits on the junction, so it blocks reflux from the junction itself. Filling that continues under the pressure must enter somewhere else.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The junction is the pressed site, but the question asks what keeps refilling while the pressure is on, which is a different question.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the deep veins are what the tourniquet tests examine, so deep disease feels like the cause.
But this pattern is a junction-and-perforator test. Deep obstruction shows up on walking with a tourniquet, not on standing with the junction pressed.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Deep obstruction is a walking test, so keep it separate from a standing test with the junction pressed.

say.text: Yes. Pressing the junction stops reflux from above, so filling that continues under the pressure must come through an incompetent perforator.
Worked case, every step shown. Step 1: raise the leg so the veins empty. Step 2: press over the saphenofemoral junction. Step 3: the patient stands, and you watch the veins.
Step 4: release the junction. Rapid filling from above means junctional incompetence. Filling that stays while the pressure is on points to the perforators. This is the Brodie–Trendelenburg test.
Second patient, same steps: the veins empty, the junction is pressed, and the patient stands. Nothing refills while the pressure is still on.
You release the junction, and the veins refill rapidly from above. Which structure is incompetent?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Only the junction was pressed. Ask where the blood came from once that pressure was released.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because perforators are the vessels that do fill the superficial veins, so they feel like the answer to any filling.
But that filling pattern belongs to the moment the pressure is still on. Here nothing refilled under the pressure, so look at the pattern after release.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Match the pattern to the moment: filling under pressure belongs to one structure, filling after release to the other.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the deep veins are what the walking tests examine, so a refill problem feels deep.
But this refill pattern is the junction test. Deep obstruction is read with a tourniquet and walking, not with the junction pressed.
Yes. Nothing refilled under the pressure, so the blood was blocked at the junction. Rapid refilling from above on release points to junctional incompetence.
A 46-year-old with varicose veins. A tourniquet goes on the thigh and she walks. Her calf aches, and the bulging veins do not empty.
Which test was done, and what does the result mean?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Walking with a tourniquet on tests the deep system. Blocked deep veins cannot empty on walking. Which name goes with the walking test?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the two test names are easy to swap, and the junction is the site you already know them for.
But the junction test compresses the junction and watches the veins on standing. This patient was walked with a tourniquet on, which is a different maneuver.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The two names are easy to swap, so match each name to its own maneuver before you trust it.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the test name is right, and the result feels like it belongs to the junction.
But a walking test with a tourniquet reads the deep veins, so the junction is the wrong thing to name here. Look at what the pain and bulging say.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The name is right; the error lies in the meaning you attached to it.

say.text: Perthes: tourniquet on, the patient walks. Veins empty if the deep veins are open and the perforators competent. Calf pain and bulging veins mean the deep veins are blocked.
Brodie–Trendelenburg is the other test: compress the junction, stand, and watch. Rapid refilling from above means junctional incompetence.
Yes. Pain and bulging on walking with the tourniquet on mean the deep veins are blocked, which is what the Perthes test reads.
You want the surgery that flush-ties the great saphenous vein at the junction, through a groin incision.
Which Trendelenburg is it?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the Brodie–Trendelenburg name is the one you use most at the bedside, so it sticks to every Trendelenburg.
But that name is a bedside test for junctional reflux. Read the noun that follows the name, because it says what is done.

sure_note.text: You were sure the bedside name fits the surgery. A test and an operation are different things, so check the noun first.

choices.label: Show me the four side by side

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a sign is something you find on examination, so the word feels like a finding about the vein.
But the Trendelenburg sign is hip abductor weakness, a finding in the standing leg that has nothing to do with the vein.

choices.label: Show me the four side by side

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the posture is used when you set up the bedside test, so it feels like part of the procedure.
But the Trendelenburg position is a body posture, not a vein procedure.

choices.label: Show me the four side by side

say.text: Four names, one word each. Brodie–Trendelenburg: a bedside test for junctional reflux. Trendelenburg sign: hip abductor weakness.
Trendelenburg position: a body posture. Trendelenburg operation: flush ligation of the great saphenous at the junction.
Yes. The Trendelenburg operation is flush ligation of the great saphenous at the junction, with its tributaries tied as well.
A patient is listed for varicose vein treatment. You need the one test that is the investigation of choice.
Which test do you order?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test shows the reflux, the perforators and the deep veins together, not just one of them.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because a bedside Doppler finds junctional reflux quickly, so it feels like the whole investigation.
But it is a screening step that stops at the junction. It does not map the whole limb.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A bedside Doppler is a screen; the question asks for the full map, so check what the test reports.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because venography is the classic picture of the deep veins, so it feels like the gold standard for everything.
But venography is reserved for complex deep disease or planned deep intervention, not the routine work-up for varicose veins.
Think of a ladder. Hand-held Doppler detects junctional reflux at the bedside, and stops there.
Colour duplex maps the reflux, the perforators and deep patency in one scan. Venography is for planned deep intervention.

choices.label: Go on to the next question

say.text: Yes. Colour duplex is the investigation of choice, because one scan shows reflux anatomy, perforators and deep patency.
Before you plan junctional surgery, the junction, the perforators and the deep veins all need examining. You want one test that covers all three.
Which one?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

K1.text: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous, elongated superficial veins; in CEAP they are veins **≥3 mm** in diameter measured standing.

K2.text: The **great saphenous vein (GSV)** system is the most commonly affected, and **saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) incompetence** is the most common site of reflux.

K3.text: **Duplex ultrasound (colour Doppler)** is the investigation of choice for varicose veins.

K4.text: **Brodie–Trendelenburg test** detects SFJ incompetence; **Perthes test** checks deep vein patency.

K5.text: **Endovenous thermal ablation** (radiofrequency or laser) is the current first-line treatment for truncal saphenous reflux; ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy is next, and open surgery is used if both are unsuitable.

K6.text: **Trendelenburg operation** = flush ligation of the GSV at the SFJ with ligation of all its tributaries.

K7.text: The GSV is stripped only to just below the knee to avoid **saphenous nerve** injury.

K8.text: Short saphenous vein surgery risks the **sural nerve**.

K9.text: **Venous ulcers** occur in the **gaiter area**, most commonly just above the **medial malleolus**.

K10.text: Compression for a venous ulcer requires an **ABPI ≥0.8** to exclude significant arterial disease.

K11.text: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous and elongated superficial veins with incompetent valves.

K12.text: In the CEAP classification, varicose veins (C2) are subcutaneous veins **≥3 mm** in diameter in the upright position.

K13.text: Telangiectasias (<1 mm) and reticular veins (1–3 mm) form CEAP class C1.

K14.text: **Great (long) saphenous vein:** begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, runs **anterior to the medial malleolus**, ascends on the medial side of leg and thigh, and joins the **femoral vein** at the SFJ through the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis) inferolateral to the **pubic tubercle**.

K16.text: The **saphenous nerve** accompanies the GSV in the leg below the knee.

K18.text: **Short (small) saphenous vein:** begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, runs **behind the lateral malleolus**, and usually joins the **popliteal vein** at the saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ) in the popliteal fossa.

K19.text: The **sural nerve** accompanies the short saphenous vein.

K21.text: **Perforating veins** connect superficial to deep veins, and their valves normally allow flow only from superficial to deep.

K22.text: **Cockett** — Medial lower leg/ankle; connect the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins

K23.text: **Boyd** — Medial leg just below the knee

K27.text: **Primary varicose veins** (most common) arise from intrinsic weakness of the vein wall and valves without a deep venous cause.

K28.text: **Secondary varicose veins** follow deep vein thrombosis (post-thrombotic), pelvic masses or pregnancy obstructing venous outflow, arteriovenous fistula, or congenital malformations such as **Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome**.

K32.text: Valve incompetence allows **reflux** (retrograde flow) of blood from deep to superficial veins or down the superficial trunks.

K33.text: Normally the **calf muscle pump** lowers venous pressure in the leg during walking.

K34.text: With reflux or deep obstruction, pressure fails to fall on walking, causing **ambulatory venous hypertension**.

K35.text: Sustained venous hypertension causes capillary leak of fluid, red cells and fibrinogen, with leukocyte trapping and inflammation, leading to oedema, skin changes and ulceration.

K36.text: **Haemosiderin** from extravasated red cells causes the brown skin pigmentation.

K37.text: Symptoms include **aching, heaviness, itching, cramps and ankle swelling**, worse after prolonged standing and at the end of the day, and relieved by **leg elevation**.

K40.text: **Lipodermatosclerosis** is induration and fibrosis of skin and subcutaneous fat of the lower leg, giving an **"inverted champagne bottle"** leg shape.

K42.text: **Corona phlebectatica** is a fan of small intradermal veins around the ankle and foot.

K43.text: **Saphena varix** is a dilatation of the GSV at the SFJ that disappears on lying down, has a **cough impulse** and a **fluid thrill on tapping**, and is a differential for **femoral hernia**.

K44.text: **Brodie–Trendelenburg test** — Leg elevated, veins emptied, SFJ compressed, patient stands. Rapid filling from above on release of pressure = **SFJ incompetence**; filling with pressure still on = **perforator** incompetence

K46.text: **Perthes test** — Tourniquet applied, patient walks/exercises; veins empty if **deep veins are patent** and perforators competent; increased pain and distension suggest **deep vein obstruction**

K48.text: **Cough impulse (Morrissey's)** — Impulse at the SFJ on coughing indicates SFJ incompetence

K51.text: A positive Perthes test (deep vein obstruction) is a **contraindication** to superficial vein ligation or stripping, because superficial veins are then acting as collaterals.

K52.text: **Duplex ultrasound** is the **investigation of choice**, showing the anatomy of reflux, junctional incompetence, perforators and deep vein patency.

K54.text: Hand-held Doppler can detect junctional reflux at the bedside but has been superseded by duplex.

K55.text: **Venography** is not routine and is reserved for complex deep venous disease or planned deep venous intervention.

K57.text: **ABPI** should be measured before compression therapy to exclude arterial disease.

K62.text: C4 — Skin changes: C4a pigmentation or eczema; C4b lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche; C4c corona phlebectatica

K68.text: Conservative measures are leg elevation, exercise, weight reduction and avoiding prolonged standing.

K69.text: **Graduated compression stockings** relieve symptoms and are used when intervention is unsuitable or declined, in pregnancy, and after treatment.

K70.text: Compression is **contraindicated** in significant peripheral arterial disease (ABPI <0.8).

K71.text: NICE advises against offering compression hosiery as treatment for symptomatic varicose veins when interventional treatment is suitable.

K72.text: **Endothermal ablation** — **radiofrequency ablation (RFA)** or **endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)** — is first-line.

K73.text: **Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy** is offered if endothermal ablation is unsuitable.

K74.text: **Open surgery** (ligation and stripping) is offered if neither is suitable.

K75.text: Endothermal ablation is done under **tumescent local anaesthesia**, which also protects surrounding tissue from heat.

K78.text: Sclerotherapy injects a sclerosant that damages the endothelium so the vein fibroses and closes.

K79.text: Common sclerosants are **sodium tetradecyl sulphate (STS)** and **polidocanol**.

K80.text: **Foam sclerotherapy** (Tessari technique, mixing sclerosant with air) displaces blood and is more effective than liquid in larger veins.

K81.text: Liquid sclerotherapy is best for telangiectasias, reticular veins and small residual varicosities.

K83.text: **Trendelenburg operation:** flush ligation of the GSV at the SFJ with ligation of all tributaries, through a groin incision.

K84.text: The GSV is then **stripped** from the groin to just below the knee.

K85.text: Stripping below the knee is avoided because of the risk of **saphenous nerve** injury.

K87.text: Short saphenous incompetence is treated by **SPJ ligation** in the popliteal fossa, with risk to the **sural nerve** and the common peroneal nerve.

K89.text: Surgery for superficial varicose veins is contraindicated when the deep veins are occluded.

K90.text: **Multilayer (four-layer) compression bandaging** is the mainstay of venous ulcer treatment.

K92.text: Correcting superficial venous reflux by early endovenous ablation speeds ulcer healing and reduces recurrence (EVRA trial).

K100.text: **Saphenous nerve** injury after below-knee GSV stripping or ablation, causing numbness on the medial leg.

K101.text: **Sural nerve** injury with short saphenous surgery or ablation.

K105.text: Most commonly affected vein — Great saphenous vein

K106.text: Most common site of reflux — Saphenofemoral junction

K107.text: Most common type — Primary varicose veins

K108.text: Most common site of venous ulcer — Gaiter area, just above the medial malleolus

K110.text: First-line treatment of truncal reflux (current) — Endothermal ablation (RFA / EVLA)

K111.text: Classic surgery for SFJ incompetence — Trendelenburg operation (flush SFJ ligation) + stripping to knee

K112.text: Sclerosant commonly used — Sodium tetradecyl sulphate (or polidocanol)

K113.text: Test for deep vein patency — Perthes test

K114.text: Test for SFJ incompetence — Brodie–Trendelenburg test

K115.text: Nerve at risk, GSV stripping — Saphenous nerve

K116.text: Nerve at risk, SSV surgery — Sural nerve

K119.text: PYQs have expected **Trendelenburg operation with stripping** as the treatment of varicose veins with SFJ incompetence; current practice (NICE) is **endothermal ablation first-line**, then foam sclerotherapy, then surgery.

K120.text: Brodie–Trendelenburg is a test for **SFJ incompetence**; Perthes is a test for **deep vein patency**; do not swap them.

K121.text: The "Trendelenburg test" (varicose veins), the "Trendelenburg operation" (SFJ ligation), the Trendelenburg position and the Trendelenburg sign (hip abductor weakness) are different things.

K122.text: Dodd perforators are in the **thigh** (Hunter's canal region) while Cockett perforators are at the **ankle/lower leg**; Boyd is just **below the knee**.

K123.text: The GSV runs **in front of the medial malleolus**; the SSV runs **behind the lateral malleolus**.

K124.text: **Saphena varix** vs **femoral hernia**: both have a cough impulse, but a saphena varix has a fluid thrill on tapping and empties on lying down.

K125.text: Before stripping or ligation, deep vein patency must be confirmed (Perthes or duplex), because in deep vein occlusion the superficial veins are the collateral outflow.

K126.text: Sclerosant answers: **sodium tetradecyl sulphate** is the classic answer; polidocanol is an equally accepted modern agent.

cards.a: From deep to superficial. It lets blood pass from the superficial veins into the deep system and shuts the reverse.

cards.q: Why is the great saphenous vein stripped only to just below the knee?
cards.a: To protect the saphenous nerve, which runs with the vein below the knee.

cards.q: Where does a venous ulcer sit?

cards.q: Which bedside test detects SFJ incompetence, and which checks deep vein patency?
cards.a: Brodie-Trendelenburg detects SFJ incompetence; Perthes checks deep vein patency.

cards.q: What must be confirmed before stripping or ligating superficial veins?
cards.a: Deep vein patency, by Perthes test or duplex, because the superficial veins are the collateral outflow.

cards.q: What is the investigation of choice for varicose veins?
cards.a: Colour duplex ultrasound, which shows reflux anatomy, junctional incompetence, perforators and deep vein patency.

cards.q: What is the current first-line treatment for truncal saphenous reflux?
cards.a: Endothermal ablation by radiofrequency or laser; foam sclerotherapy next, and open surgery if both are unsuitable.

cards.q: What is done before compression for a venous ulcer?
